title: IID Monte Carlo integration and error

items.title: IID Monte Carlo sample mean, variance, and standard error
items.statement: For real IID outputs with finite first absolute moment, define the target and sample mean; for any finite real sample define the Bessel-corrected sample variance, and under a finite second moment define the population variance, standard error, and plug-in estimate.
items.strategy: State the sample mean convention from the library's partial-sum definition and give the sample-variance and standard-error formulas with their exact moment and sample-size domains.

references.title: Art B. Owen, Monte Carlo Theory, Methods and Examples, Chapter 2
references.locator: §§2.1–2.3, PDF pp. 15–22: sample mean, population and sample variance, and standard-error notation.

references.title: Rick Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed.
references.locator: §§2.2.1 and 2.2.14, printed pp. 57–58 and 64–65: IID moment conventions and sample means.

items.title: Unbiasedness and exact variance of the IID Monte Carlo mean
items.statement: For a real IID sequence, the sample mean has expectation equal to the common mean when the first absolute moment is finite; with a finite second moment its variance is exactly the population variance divided by n.
items.strategy: Use equality in law to identify each summand's moments, linearity for the mean, and variance additivity for the finite independent sample.

references.title: Art B. Owen, Monte Carlo Theory, Methods and Examples, Chapter 2
references.locator: §2.1, PDF pp. 16–17, equations (2.4)–(2.5): unbiased sample mean and exact variance scaling.

references.title: Rick Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed.
references.locator: §2.2.1, printed pp. 56–57: variance additivity for uncorrelated summands; §2.2.3, printed p. 57.

items.title: Strong and weak consistency of the IID Monte Carlo mean
items.statement: If the common real IID output has finite first absolute moment, then the sample mean converges in probability and almost surely to its expectation; in fact its mean absolute error tends to zero.
items.strategy: Apply the fully proved integrable IID weak law and Kolmogorov strong law to the sequence of integrand outputs.

references.title: Art B. Owen, Monte Carlo Theory, Methods and Examples, Chapter 2
references.locator: §2.1, PDF p. 16, equations (2.2)–(2.3): weak and strong consistency of simple Monte Carlo.

references.title: Rick Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed.
references.locator: Theorem 2.2.14, printed p. 65, and Theorem 2.4.1, printed pp. 76–78: integrable IID weak and strong laws, including proofs.

items.title: Consistency of the IID Monte Carlo sample variance
items.statement: For real IID outputs with finite second moment, the Bessel-corrected sample variance converges almost surely to the population variance; when that variance is positive, the estimated standard error is relatively consistent for sigma divided by the square root of n.
items.strategy: Apply the IID strong law to the outputs and their squares, then use the centered-squares identity and continuity of the square root.

references.title: Art B. Owen, Monte Carlo Theory, Methods and Examples, Chapter 2
references.locator: §2.2, PDF p. 19: consistency of s by applying the weak law to the sample averages of Y and Y squared.

references.title: Rick Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed.
references.locator: Theorem 2.4.1, printed pp. 76–78: strong law used for both Y and the transformed sequence Y squared.

items.title: Lindeberg–Lévy limit for the IID Monte Carlo mean
items.statement: Assuming AC, for real IID outputs with positive finite variance, the centered sample mean multiplied by the square root of n converges in distribution to the centered normal law with the population variance.
items.strategy: Apply the fully proved local Lindeberg–Lévy theorem to the sample sums, rewrite the statistic as the centered sample mean, and scale the weak limit continuously.

references.title: Art B. Owen, Monte Carlo Theory, Methods and Examples, Chapter 2
references.locator: Theorem 2.1 in §2.2, PDF p. 19: IID CLT statement; Owen cites Chung for its proof, which is not imported.

references.title: Rick Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed.
references.locator: Theorem 3.4.1, printed pp. 144–145: complete characteristic-function proof of the IID Lindeberg–Lévy theorem.

items.axiom_use: AC is explicitly assumed and is inherited from thm-lindeberg-levy-iid-central-limit-theorem and the library normal-law definition; no additional choice is used in the Monte Carlo rewrite.

title: IID Monte Carlo integration and error — Examples

items.title: Gaussian integrand: exact Monte Carlo moments and asymptotic error
items.statement: For IID normal integrand outputs with mean mu and positive variance sigma squared, the Monte Carlo mean is unbiased with variance sigma squared divided by n, its plug-in standard error is relatively consistent, and its square-root-n limit is normal under AC.
items.strategy: Use the proved normal moment supplier to check the finite-moment hypotheses, then apply the local Monte Carlo moment, sample-variance, and CLT results.

references.title: Art B. Owen, Monte Carlo Theory, Methods and Examples, Chapter 2
references.locator: §§2.1–2.2, PDF pp. 16–19: mean, variance, sample variance, and the IID CLT.

references.title: Rick Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed.
references.locator: Theorem 3.4.1, printed pp. 144–145: finite-positive-variance IID CLT.

items.axiom_use: AC is required by the normal-law interface and the local Monte Carlo CLT, and is stated in the example.

items.title: Finite mean does not give a finite-variance Monte Carlo error
items.statement: Under countable choice, the Pareto law with tail t to the power minus three halves has finite mean and infinite second moment. Any IID sample with this law has a consistent sample mean, but no finite population standard error sigma divided by the square root of n is available.
items.strategy: Construct the Pareto law from its CDF, compute the first and second moments by the layer-cake formulas, and apply the integrable IID consistency theorem while keeping finite-variance error conclusions outside their hypotheses.

references.title: Art B. Owen, Monte Carlo Theory, Methods and Examples, Chapter 2
references.locator: §2.1, PDF p. 16: finite-mean weak and strong consistency; §2.3, PDF pp. 21–22: finite-variance standard-error computation caveat.

references.title: Rick Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed.
references.locator: Theorem 2.2.14, printed p. 65: weak law under a finite first absolute moment; Theorem 2.4.1, printed pp. 76–78: strong law under the same moment condition.

items.axiom_use: Countable Choice is used for the CDF-to-law correspondence and the continuous-to-Borel and Riemann/Lebesgue bridges in the moment calculation; no full AC or dependent choice is used, and the conditional IID consistency result is choice-free.
